title: P-Sh-T

segments.voice: Yesterday, D-R-Sh: midrash, the reading that seeks and digs. Your line was seek. Did you ask the question you'd been leaving alone? Today, the other half of reading. Day one thousand four hundred.

Two eggs. That's the whole line on an old recipe card, in faded ink. A clever cook could read deep things into it, about pairs, about beginnings, about fragile shells. The cake doesn't care. The card means two eggs. Jewish reading has a name for what a text simply says, before anyone gets clever. Peshat. The plain sense. In modern Hebrew, the same root gives pashut, simple, the word people use for easy, obvious. Today's root: pey, shin, tet. P-Sh-T. Yesterday the rabbis dug. Today they make sure the ground is still there.
screen: `TWO EGGS. JUST TWO EGGS.` → `PASHUT: SIMPLE.` → `P-SH-T: THE PLAIN SENSE.`

segments.voice: Turn this root four ways. First, the cloth. In the Bible's Hebrew, the verb from this root has to do with spreading out and stripping off. When Joseph's brothers take his coat from him, the verb is this one. Peshat, in that light, is a text with nothing laid over it, flat and in plain view. Second, the anchor. The Talmud, in tractate Shabbat, sets down a short rule: a verse does not leave its plain meaning. Midrash can soar, but it can't cut the rope. Whatever else a verse is made to say, it still says what it says. Even the boldest reading has to come home to the words on the page. Third, the commentator. Rashi, a medieval commentator, says on a verse in Genesis that he has come only for the plain sense, and for those teachings that help the words make sense. Word by word, plainly. Fourth, the floor. Later Jewish teachers described levels of reading, and peshat is the floor everything else stands on. Above it come hints, seeking, and secrets. But nobody climbs without a floor. Look back over the week and the roots make a path: creating and forming, wisdom and command, walking, seeking, and now the plain. Six days of digging into words, and the seventh says: before you dig, read what's there.
screen: `THE CLOTH: NOTHING LAID OVER IT.` · `THE ANCHOR: A VERSE KEEPS ITS PLAIN SENSE.` · `THE COMMENTATOR: RASHI'S PLAIN SENSE.` · `THE FLOOR: EVERYTHING STANDS ON IT.` · then, large: `פְּשָׁט`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one verse plainly. Here is one, from the first chapter of Genesis: "And God said: 'Let there be light.' And there was light." Settle, and breathe. Say it to yourself slowly. Then resist every urge to explain it. No symbolism, no theory, no lesson. Just what it says. Someone spoke. Light was. Notice what the plain words do on their own. Then let the verse rest, and let yourself rest with it. The bell holds the time.
P-Sh-T. Pey, shin, tet: the root of peshat, the plain sense of a text, and of pashut, simple. Today's word.
Your line: plain. Today, when someone tells you something, hear what they actually said before you decide what they meant. Day one thousand four hundred.

howItsDone: Jewish students traditionally learn the Torah with Rashi's commentary, which aims at the plain sense, and Jewish tradition holds that a verse never departs from its peshat even when it is also read through midrash.
